facts: Aconcagua, in the Argentine Andes, is the highest mountain outside Asia at 6,961 metres, and the highest point in both the Western and Southern hemispheres.
Argentina stretches from subtropical forest in the north to the sub-Antarctic tip of Tierra del Fuego.
Its border with Chile, running along the Andes, is the third longest international border in the world.
AR.about: At the heart of Argentina lie the Pampas, flat and fertile grasslands that made the country one of the great exporters of beef and grain from the late 19th century. North of them stretches the hot, scrubby Gran Chaco, while the north-east holds subtropical forest and the Iguazú Falls on the border with Brazil. To the south, Patagonia is a windswept steppe of plateaus ending at the Andes, where glaciers such as Perito Moreno descend into turquoise lakes. The independence movement began with the May Revolution of 1810 in Buenos Aires, and independence was formally declared at Tucumán on 9 July 1816. Millions of European immigrants, especially from Italy and Spain, arrived between the 1870s and 1930s, shaping the language, food and urban culture. Roughly a third of Argentines live in Greater Buenos Aires on the Río de la Plata. The country maintains its claim to the Falkland Islands, over which it fought Britain in 1982.

facts: Bolivia has two capitals: Sucre is the constitutional seat and La Paz holds the government.
The Salar de Uyuni is the largest salt flat in the world and holds a large share of global lithium reserves.
It lost its coastline to Chile in the 19th century and still maintains a navy on Lake Titicaca.
BO.about: Most Bolivians live on or near the Altiplano, a high plateau averaging around 3,700 metres between two ranges of the Andes, or in the temperate valleys and steep subtropical Yungas below it. Yet more than half the country is eastern lowland, part Amazonian forest and part Chaco scrub, where Santa Cruz has grown into the largest city on the back of agriculture and natural gas. The ruins of Tiwanaku near Lake Titicaca recall a powerful pre-Inca civilisation, and under Spain the silver mountain of Cerro Rico at Potosí was one of the richest sources of wealth in the empire. Independence came on 6 August 1825, and the country took its name from Simón Bolívar. It later lost territory to Paraguay in the Chaco War of 1932–35. Bolivia has one of the largest Indigenous population shares in the Americas, mainly Quechua and Aymara, recognised in the 2009 constitution that defined it as a plurinational state.

facts: Brazil borders every South American country except Chile and Ecuador.
It holds about 60% of the Amazon rainforest and the largest river by discharge in the world.
Brasília was built from nothing in the 1950s and inaugurated as the capital in 1960.
BR.about: Beyond the Amazon basin, Brazil takes in the Brazilian Highlands, the vast Cerrado savanna, the Pantanal, one of the world's largest tropical wetlands, and what remains of the Atlantic Forest along a coastline of more than 7,000 kilometres. Portugal claimed the territory after Pedro Álvares Cabral landed in 1500, and the colony grew rich successively on brazilwood, sugar worked by enslaved Africans and, in the 18th century, gold and diamonds from Minas Gerais. When Napoleon invaded Portugal in 1808 the royal court moved to Rio de Janeiro, and in 1822 the prince regent Pedro declared independence, founding an empire that lasted until the republic of 1889. Brazil was the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery, in 1888. It is the largest Portuguese-speaking nation, with most people living near the coast, and São Paulo is its economic powerhouse. Soybeans, iron ore, beef, coffee and aircraft manufacturing are among its major industries.

facts: Chile runs over 4,300 kilometres north to south but averages under 180 kilometres wide.
The Atacama Desert is the driest non-polar place on Earth, with some weather stations never recording rain.
Ojos del Salado is the highest active volcano in the world.
CL.about: Between the Andes and the Pacific, Chile passes through almost every climate on the continent. The arid north holds some of the world's richest copper deposits, making Chile the largest copper producer on Earth. The central valley, with a Mediterranean climate, is the farming and wine heartland and home to most of the population, while further south come lakes, forests and snow-capped volcanoes, then a fragmented coast of fjords, islands and ice fields in Patagonia. Chile also governs Easter Island, or Rapa Nui, a Polynesian island far out in the Pacific annexed in 1888. Independence was proclaimed in 1818 after victories led by Bernardo O'Higgins and José de San Martín. In the War of the Pacific of 1879–84 Chile took the nitrate-rich north from Peru and Bolivia. Lying above an active subduction zone, the country is prone to major earthquakes; the 1960 Valdivia earthquake is the most powerful ever recorded.

facts: Colombia is the only South American country with coastlines on both the Pacific and the Caribbean.
It is the second most biodiverse country in the world and has more bird species than any other.
The Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta rises to 5,700 metres within 50 kilometres of the sea.
CO.about: In Colombia the Andes split into three separate ranges, divided by the long valleys of the Magdalena and Cauca rivers, and it is in these highlands that most people live, in cities such as Bogotá, Medellín and Cali. To the east the land opens onto the Llanos grasslands and then the Amazon forest, while the Pacific lowlands of Chocó are among the rainiest places on Earth. Independence from Spain was declared in 1810 and secured by Simón Bolívar's victory at Boyacá in 1819. Colombia formed the core of Gran Colombia, which broke apart around 1830, and it lost Panama in 1903. The country is famous for its mild Arabica coffee grown on Andean slopes, and it is a leading source of emeralds and cut flowers, with oil and coal also important exports. Decades of internal armed conflict involving guerrilla groups, paramilitaries and drug cartels shaped modern history, and a peace agreement with the FARC was signed in 2016.

facts: Because of the equatorial bulge, Chimborazo's summit is the farthest point on the surface from the Earth's centre.
Ecuador was the first country to write rights of nature into its constitution, in 2008.
The Galápagos Islands, roughly 1,000 kilometres offshore, shaped Darwin's theory of natural selection.
EC.about: Named after the equator that crosses it just north of the capital, Ecuador divides into three mainland regions: the Pacific coastal lowlands, the Andean highlands, and the Amazonian east known as the Oriente. The Andes here form a double row of volcanoes, including snow-capped Cotopaxi, a corridor nicknamed the Avenue of the Volcanoes. The highlands were absorbed into the Inca Empire shortly before the Spanish conquest of the 1530s. Independence came after the Battle of Pichincha in 1822, when the territory joined Gran Colombia, and Ecuador became a separate republic in 1830. Guayaquil, the busy Pacific port, is the largest city and economic centre, while Quito is the political and cultural capital. Ecuador is the world's leading exporter of bananas and a major exporter of shrimp and cut roses, oil has been a leading export since the 1970s, and the so-called Panama hat is actually woven in Ecuador from toquilla palm.

facts: Guyana is the only South American country with English as its official language.
Kaieteur Falls drops 226 metres in a single uninterrupted plunge, roughly four times the height of Niagara.
Large offshore oil discoveries after 2015 made it one of the fastest-growing economies in the world.
GY.about: The name Guyana is usually explained as an Indigenous word meaning 'land of many waters', and the country is laced with rivers such as the Essequibo, Demerara and Berbice. Most people live on a narrow coastal plain that lies partly below high-tide level, protected by sea walls and drainage canals first built by Dutch colonists. Inland, the land rises through dense rainforest to the Pakaraima Mountains and the open Rupununi savanna near the Brazilian border. The Dutch founded plantation colonies here in the 17th century, and Britain took control in the early 19th century, uniting them as British Guiana in 1831. After slavery ended, indentured labourers came from India, and Indo-Guyanese now form the largest group, alongside Afro-Guyanese, Amerindian and mixed communities. Independence came on 26 May 1966, and Guyana became a republic in 1970. Venezuela maintains a long-standing claim to the Essequibo region, about two-thirds of the territory. Sugar, rice, bauxite and gold have been traditional exports.

facts: Paraguay is one of only two landlocked countries in South America, along with Bolivia.
The Itaipú Dam, shared with Brazil, is among the largest hydroelectric plants in the world and supplies most of Paraguay's power.
Guaraní is an official language alongside Spanish and is spoken by most of the population.
PY.about: The Paraguay River divides the country into two sharply different halves. East of the river lies the Región Oriental, a region of rolling hills, forest and fertile farmland where the great majority of people live. To the west stretches the Gran Chaco, a hot, dry plain of thorny scrub occupying more than half the territory but home to only a small fraction of the population, including Mennonite farming colonies founded in the 20th century. In the 17th and 18th centuries Jesuit missionaries organised Guaraní communities into mission towns, or reductions, whose ruins at Trinidad and Jesús are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Paraguay declared independence from Spain in 1811. The War of the Triple Alliance against Brazil, Argentina and Uruguay from 1864 to 1870 killed a very large share of its population, while the Chaco War with Bolivia in the 1930s ended in victory. Soybeans, beef and exported hydroelectricity now drive the economy.

facts: Machu Picchu, built in the 15th century, was never found by the Spanish and stayed largely unknown outside the region until 1911.
Peru shares Lake Titicaca with Bolivia, the highest navigable lake in the world.
The potato was domesticated in the Peruvian Andes, where thousands of varieties are still grown.
PE.about: Peru has three contrasting regions. A narrow desert coast, kept dry by the cold Humboldt Current, is broken by river oases where most people live; the same current feeds one of the world's richest fisheries, based on anchoveta, which collapses when El Niño brings warm water. Inland rise the high Andes, and to the east more than half the country is Amazon rainforest, including the headwaters of the Amazon itself. Civilisation here is ancient: Caral, on the coast, is one of the oldest cities in the Americas, and later cultures such as the Nazca, Moche and Chimú preceded the Inca Empire centred on Cusco. Francisco Pizarro's conquest began in 1532, and Lima became the seat of Spain's richest South American viceroyalty. José de San Martín proclaimed independence in 1821, secured by the Battle of Ayacucho in 1824. Mining of copper, gold and silver is the backbone of exports, and Peruvian cuisine has gained international renown.

facts: Suriname is the smallest sovereign state in South America, both by land area and by population.
Dutch is the official language, the only country in the Americas where that is the case.
More than 90% of the country is still covered by rainforest.
SR.about: Suriname's land rises from a swampy coastal plain through a belt of sandy savanna to forested interior uplands. The Afobaka Dam on the Suriname River, built in the 1960s to power aluminium smelting, created the Brokopondo Reservoir, one of the largest artificial lakes in the world. England founded the first lasting colony, but in 1667 the Treaty of Breda confirmed the Dutch in possession, with New Amsterdam, now New York, staying in English hands. Plantation slavery was brutal, and many escaped Africans founded Maroon societies such as the Saramaka and Ndyuka deep in the forest, whose descendants still live along the rivers. After abolition in 1863, contract workers arrived from India, Java and China, giving the country one of the most ethnically mixed populations in the Americas, with Sranan Tongo as a common language. Independence came on 25 November 1975, prompting large emigration to the Netherlands. Gold, oil and formerly bauxite dominate exports.

facts: Uruguay generates the large majority of its electricity from renewable sources, chiefly wind and hydro.
It won the first FIFA World Cup, hosted at home in 1930.
Roughly half the national population lives in the Montevideo metropolitan area.
UY.about: Uruguay is a country without real mountains: its landscape is gently rolling grassland broken by low ridges called cuchillas, drained by the Río Negro and bounded by the Uruguay River and the wide estuary of the Río de la Plata. A long Atlantic shoreline of beaches and lagoons runs to the Brazilian border, with Punta del Este as its best-known resort. Known in colonial times as the Banda Oriental, the territory was fought over by Spain and Portugal and later occupied by Brazil, before independence was confirmed in 1828 with British mediation, creating a buffer state between its larger neighbours; its first constitution followed in 1830. In the early 20th century, governments led by José Batlle y Ordóñez built one of the earliest welfare states in the Americas. Cattle and sheep greatly outnumber people, and beef, soybeans, wood pulp and dairy are leading exports, while the country is noted for political stability and a strong middle class.

facts: Angel Falls drops 979 metres, the tallest uninterrupted waterfall in the world.
Venezuela holds the largest proven oil reserves of any country.
Lake Maracaibo sees near-nightly lightning storms, among the most frequent anywhere on Earth.
VE.about: Explorers sailing along the Caribbean coast in 1499 saw Indigenous houses built on stilts over Lake Maracaibo, and the name Venezuela, meaning 'little Venice', is traditionally traced to that sight. The country takes in a northern arm of the Andes around Mérida, the coastal ranges where Caracas lies, the vast Llanos plains crossed by the Orinoco River, and in the south-east the Guiana Highlands, where flat-topped sandstone mountains called tepuis rise abruptly from the forest. Independence was declared on 5 July 1811, and Simón Bolívar, born in Caracas, secured it with the victory at Carabobo in 1821; Venezuela left Gran Colombia to become a separate republic in 1830. The discovery of large oil fields in the early 20th century transformed a largely agricultural country into a petroleum economy, with oil long providing most export earnings. A severe economic and political crisis from the mid-2010s led millions of Venezuelans to emigrate.
